t: Variable Names
What you will learn
A **variable** is a name that holds a value so you can use it later. You will learn the rules for naming one, which names Python rejects, and how to pick names that make your code easy to read.

**On the AP exam:** the exam writes a variable like this: `score ← 10`. The arrow ← means the same thing as `=` in Python: store the value on the right into the name on the left. The same naming ideas apply: a clear name, no spaces.

House rules: keep ALL of your work

Your teacher grades the code you submit, so your earlier work has to stay in the box as proof. **Never delete code.** When you are done with some code, or fix it, or replace it, **comment it out** instead.
Commenting out
Select the lines and press **Ctrl + /**. A `#` goes in front of each line, the line turns gray, Python skips it, and it stays there.
Press **Ctrl + /** again to turn it back on.
When you fix a line
Comment out the old version and type the new version on the line **right below** it.
The two kinds of comments
Each step tells you exactly which kind to write and where. Follow it exactly.
1. Heading comment
A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code. It is a title for a whole section, like `# Step 3` or `# Ride checker`.
2. End-of-line comment
Every other comment goes on the **SAME line** as the code it explains, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`. An explaining comment never goes on its own line above or below.
Do exactly what each step says. A comment that doesn't explain anything, like `#comment`, earns no credit.
How do I comment out everything above?
What it does

A **comment** is a line that starts with `#`. Python skips it completely, but it stays in your code box so your teacher can see it. Commenting out your old code keeps your work and keeps your output short.
Step by step
Click once **inside the code box** so the blinking cursor is there.
Press **Ctrl + A**. Everything in the box turns blue (selected).
Press **Ctrl + /** (the slash key). A `#` appears at the start of every line.
Click at the very bottom of the code box and start your heading comment, like `# Step 5`.
What it looks like
Only the lines that start with `#` are skipped. Your new code at the bottom (no `#`) is the only code that runs.
If something goes wrong
**Nothing happened?** Click inside the code box first, then try again.
**Pressed it twice by accident?** Press **Ctrl + /** again and your code turns back on. Your `# Step` headings stay as comments.
You never need to delete code. If you did delete something by mistake, type it again and comment it out.
Heading comment and end-of-line comment: what is the difference?
Both are comments (they start with `#`). The only difference is **where** you put them.
1. Heading comment: its own line, ABOVE the code
2. End-of-line comment: on the SAME line, after the code
Leave a few spaces before the `#` on an end-of-line comment. And a comment must say something. A comment like `#comment` earns no credit because it doesn't explain anything.

"Add an end-of-line comment at the end of each print line"

"Put a heading comment ABOVE the program"
A `#` line on its own, above all the lines of that program.
How do I write a prediction?
A **prediction** is your guess of what Python will show, written **before** you run the code. It makes you think first, and Python then tells you if you were right.
Step by step
Look at one line, like `print(7 // 2)`.
Work out the answer in your head or on paper.
Type your answer at the end of the line, after a few spaces: `print(7 // 2)   # my guess: 3`.
Do that for every line **before** you click Run.
Click Run and compare. If a guess was wrong, that's great: it means you learned something.
Wrong guesses cost you nothing. The check only needs a comment on the line, so write your honest guess.

Errors are Python telling you exactly what it couldn't do. They are not a sign that you're bad at this. Even professional programmers see them all day.

How do I print words and a number together?
There are two ways. Both give the same result.
1. A comma (the easy way)
Python adds a space between the pieces for you, and it works with any kind of value.
2. Plus and str()
`+` only joins text to text. So a number has to be turned into text first with `str()`. You also have to type the space yourself.
`print("Whole minutes: " + 2)` crashes with a TypeError, because `+` can't join text and a number.
What is a variable?
A **variable** is a name that holds a value, like a labeled box. You put something in the box once, and then you can use the label whenever you need what's inside.
`player_name` is the label on the box.
`"Sam"` is what you put in the box.
`print(player_name)` opens the box and shows what's inside: **Sam**.
Python remembers the value for the rest of the program, so you only type it once.
Why does the name go on the LEFT of the = sign?
In Python the single `=` is **not** "equals". It means **store**: take the value on the right and put it into the name on the left.
`"Sam" = player_name` is backwards, and Python will show an error.
Read `x = 5` as "x gets 5" or "store 5 in x".
What does print() do?
`print()` shows something in the **Output** box on the right. Whatever you put inside the brackets is what gets shown.

What is the difference between print(player_name) and print("player_name")?
The quotes change what Python prints.
print(player_name)
Sam
no quotes: Python opens the variable and prints what's inside
print("player_name")

quotes: Python prints the exact words you typed
Quotes mean: "this is just text, don't look it up."
No quotes means: "this is a name, go find its value."
Why does my name need quotes?
Text (like a name) goes inside quotes so Python knows it's **text**, not the name of a variable.
Without quotes you get `NameError: name 'Sam' is not defined`. Python thinks Sam is a variable you forgot to make.
Single quotes `'Sam'` and double quotes `"Sam"` both work. Just use the same kind at both ends.

With quotes, Python prints the words you typed.
Without quotes, Python prints what's stored in the variable.

Why does Python have naming rules?
Python has to be able to tell a variable name apart from numbers, math symbols, and its own special words. The rules keep it from getting confused.
A name starting with a digit could look like a number.
A dash could look like subtraction.
A space would make Python think there are two separate names.
What is a Python keyword?
A **keyword** is a word Python already uses for its own grammar. You are not allowed to use it as a variable name.
`class = 5` fails because Python thinks you're starting a class.
In the editor, keywords are colored purple. If your variable name turns purple, pick a different name.

Python treats capital and lowercase letters as **different letters**. So these are three different variables:
If you make `pizza_slices` and then type `Pizza_slices` later, Python says it doesn't exist.
The easiest habit: always type variable names in lowercase.

**Syntax** means grammar. Python read your line and couldn't understand it because it breaks a grammar rule.
For a bad variable name, it means the name broke one of the naming rules (a space, a symbol, a keyword).
A SyntaxError is a good sign in this step. It means Python rejected the name, which is exactly what you're testing for.

How can a variable change?
A variable holds **one value at a time**. When you store something new in it, the old value is gone.
That's why they're called variables: the value can vary.
Why does lives = lives - 1 work? Isn't that impossible in math?
In math, `lives = lives - 1` would be impossible. But in Python the `=` is not "equals". It means **store**.
What Python does
Work out the **right side** first: `lives - 1` is 3 - 1, which is 2.
Then store that answer into the name on the **left**: `lives`.
Now `lives` holds 2.
Right side first, then store it on the left. Always.

**Why use the comma?** It is the quickest way to show mixed types. You do not need `str()`, you do not have to remember the spaces, and nothing crashes when a number is mixed in with text. Use it when you just want to **display** values.

**Pitfalls of the comma:** (1) It always puts exactly one space between the pieces, so you cannot get `Level:7` or `$5` with it. `print("$", 5)` shows `$ 5`. (2) It only works inside `print()`. The two kinds of comments
Each step tells you exactly which kind to write and where. Follow it exactly.
1. Heading comment
A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code. It is a title for a whole section, like `# Step 3` or `# Ride checker`.
2. End-of-line comment
Every other comment goes on the **SAME line** as the code it explains, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`. An explaining comment never goes on its own line above or below.

What does // actually do?

`//` is called **floor division**. It divides two numbers, then **throws away everything after the decimal point**. It answers one question: **how many whole times does the second number fit into the first?**
Picture it
You have 7 cookies and each bag holds 2. You can fill **3 whole bags**, and 1 cookie is left over. `7 // 2` gives you the 3: the number of whole bags.
More examples
2 fits into 7 three whole times
2 fits into 10 exactly five times
4 does not fit into 1 even once
7 fits 14 whole times (7 x 14 = 98)
`//` never gives you a decimal part. Whatever would come after the decimal point is just dropped.
Try it (click to see the answer)

3  (6 x 3 = 18, and 6 x 4 = 24 is too big)
0  (10 does not fit into 5)
Why is 7 // 2 equal to 3 and not 3.5?
Python divides 7 by 2. The real answer is **3.5**.
`//` then rounds **down** to the whole number below: **3**.
The `.5` is thrown away. It is not rounded up.
`//` does **not** round to the nearest number. Even `3.9` would become `3`. It always goes down.

Ask the question `//` asks: **how many whole times does 4 fit into 1?**
Picture 1 cookie and bags that each hold 4. You cannot fill even one bag, so you fill **0 bags**.
Rule: if the first number is **smaller** than the second, `//` gives **0**.

Why does 7.5 // 2 show 3.0 and not 3?
Both `7 // 2` and `7.5 // 2` round down to the same amount: **3**. The only difference is how Python **stores** the answer.
Two kinds of numbers
An **integer** holds whole numbers only, so it prints with no point: `3`.
A **float** can hold a decimal part, so it always prints with a point, even when the decimal part is zero: `3.0`.

both are integers, so the answer is an integer
7.5 is a float, so the answer is a float
`3.0` is exactly three. There is no decimal part hiding. Only the **container** is different.

Modulus: The Remainder ( % )
What you will learn

**Modulus**, written `%`, gives the **remainder**: what is LEFT OVER after you divide as many whole times as you can. It is NOT a percent sign here. **On the AP exam:** modulus is written `a MOD b` and it is on almost every exam. Tip: click **% Modulus** in the Math key above the code any time you want a reminder.

Problem 1 walkthrough: Reassigning variables
Take it **one line at a time**, and keep a small table of what each variable equals after every line. Here is the program:
**The trace table:**
**Step by step:**
`a = 4`: a is 4. b and c do not exist yet.
`b = a * 2`: use the value a has right now (4), so b is 8.
`a = b - 3`: use b (8): 8 - 3 = 5. Now a is 5. The old 4 is gone. b stays 8, because b was already calculated and does not change when a changes.
`c = a + b`: use the NEW a (5) and b (8), so c is 13.
`print(a, b, c)` shows the three current values: 5 8 13.
Answer: **C (5 8 13)**. Variables always hold their **latest** value. Choice A and D keep the old a = 4, and choice B uses the old a when adding for c.
Problem 2 walkthrough: Order matters
Take it **one line at a time**, and keep a small table of what each variable equals after every line. Here is the program:
**The trace table:**
**Step by step:**
`x = 10` and `y = 3`: x is 10, y is 3.
`x = x // y`: 10 // 3 is 3 (3 fits into 10 three whole times; the decimal is dropped). x becomes 3.
`y = x + y`: x is **3 now**, not 10. So y = 3 + 3 = 6.
`x = x % y`: 3 % 6 is 3. (6 does not fit into 3 at all, so the whole 3 is the remainder.) x stays 3.
`print(x, y)` shows 3 6.
Answer: **B (3 6)**. The most common mistake is using x = 10 on the `y = x + y` line (that gives 13). Always use the value a variable has **at that moment**.

Problem 5 walkthrough: Order of operations
Take it **one line at a time**, and keep a small table of what each variable equals after every line. Here is the program:
**The trace table:**
**Step by step:**
`/`, `//`, `*` and `%` all have the **same priority**, and they are done **before** `+`. Operators of the same priority go left to right.
So the + splits the line into two parts: `a / b` on the left and `a // b * a % b` on the right.
Left part: 7 / 2 = 3.5.
Right part, left to right: `a // b` = 7 // 2 = 3. Then `3 * a` = 21. Then `21 % b` = 21 % 2 = 1 (21 is odd, so the remainder is 1).

Answer: **B (4.5)**. Mixing `/` with `//`, `*` and `%` is tricky: group the same-priority operators and work left to right.

The two kinds of comments
Each step tells you exactly which kind to write and where. Follow it exactly.
1. Heading comment
A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code. It is a title for a whole section, like `# Step 3` or `# Ride checker`.
2. End-of-line comment
Every other comment goes on the **SAME line** as the code it explains, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`. An explaining comment never goes on its own line above or below.
Do exactly what each step says. A comment that doesn't explain anything, like `#comment`, earns no credit.

A **comment** is a line that starts with `#`. Python skips it completely, but it stays in your code box so your teacher can see it. Commenting out your old code keeps your work and keeps your output short.

If Statements
What you will learn

Until now your programs ran every line, top to bottom, every time. An **`if` statement** lets a program **decide**: run some lines only when a condition is `True`, and skip them when it is `False`. You will learn how to write one, how **indentation** shows which lines belong to it, how to use Boolean variables and `and`/`or`/`not` as conditions, how an `if` can change a variable, how several `if` statements work together, how to put one `if` inside another, and how to put it all together in a ticket price program.

**On the AP exam:** the exam writes an `if` statement as `IF (condition)` followed by a block of lines in curly braces `{ }`. It is the first of the three building blocks of every program (sequence, selection, and iteration), and *selection* is exactly what `if` does. Tracing which lines run is one of the most common exam questions.

If, Elif, and Else
What you will learn

A plain `if` only says what to do when something is `True`. Often you also need to say what to do **otherwise**, or to choose between **three or more** options. You will learn `else` (the "otherwise" branch), `elif` ("else if", extra choices in a chain), why the **order** of a chain matters, how an `if`/`elif` chain is different from separate `if` statements, how the exam writes it, and how to use a chain to pick a value for a variable.

**On the AP exam:** the exam has `IF` and `IF … ELSE`, but **no `ELIF`**. To pick between three or more options, the exam puts another `IF` inside the `ELSE`. You will practice reading both styles. Exactly one branch of an `IF … ELSE` always runs.

Key Events
What you will learn

In a game or an app, the program does not know ahead of time what the user will do next. The user presses a key, clicks, or taps, and the program **reacts**. This is called **event-driven programming**: the program has code that waits for an event, and runs it when the event happens.

**Pretend keyboard:** on the CodeHS graphics canvas, the canvas runs your handler for you each time a real key is pressed. This editor has no canvas, so you will make a **pretend key press** with `Event("a")` and hand it to your code yourself. Everything inside your handler is exactly the same.

**On the AP exam:** the exam has no key-event commands, but it tests the ideas behind them. An **event** is an action (a key press, a mouse click, a program starting) that **supplies input** to a program. The code that responds is a **procedure with a parameter**, written with `IF/ELSE`, string comparisons, and changing a variable. You will practice each of those, and in Step 7 you will read two procedures written the way the exam writes them.

House rules: keep ALL of your work

Your teacher grades the code you submit, so your earlier work has to stay in the box as proof. **Never delete code.** When you are done with some code, or fix it, or replace it, **comment it out** instead.
Commenting out
Select the lines and press **Ctrl + /**. A `#` goes in front of each line, the line turns gray, Python skips it, and it stays there.
Press **Ctrl + /** again to turn it back on.
When you fix a line
Comment out the old version and type the new version on the line **right below** it.
The two kinds of comments
Each step tells you exactly which kind to write and where. Follow it exactly.
1. Heading comment
A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code. It is a title for a whole section, like `# Step 3` or `# Ride checker`.
2. End-of-line comment
Every other comment goes on the **SAME line** as the code it explains, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`. An explaining comment never goes on its own line above or below.
Do exactly what each step says. A comment that doesn't explain anything, like `#comment`, earns no credit.

A **comment** is a line that starts with `#`. Python skips it completely, but it stays in your code box so your teacher can see it. Commenting out your old code keeps your work and keeps your output short.

General For Loops
What you will learn

Last time you looped over **numbers** made by `range`. A **general for loop** loops straight over the **things themselves**: every item in a **list**, or every character in a **string**. There is no counting. The loop variable becomes each real value, one at a time. You will learn how to loop over a list and a string, why the loop variable is the **value** and not a position, how to total and average a list, how to filter with an `if`, how to count letters, and how the exam writes it.

**On the AP exam:** the exam's version is `FOR EACH item IN list { }`. It is one of the most common exam loops, and it is used with lists. A **list** holds several values in order, written in square brackets with commas: `[3, 8, 5]`. Careful: the exam numbers list positions starting at **1**, but Python starts at **0**.

While Loops
What you will learn

You already know `for` loops, which repeat a set number of times or once per item. A **while loop** repeats **as long as a yes-or-no question stays `True`**. Use it when you do **not** know ahead of time how many times to repeat: counting down, adding up until you reach a goal, or asking again until an answer is right. You will learn the three jobs every while loop needs, how to avoid a loop that never ends, and how the exam writes the same idea.

**On the AP exam:** the exam has **no** `while`. Its loop is `REPEAT UNTIL(condition)`, which repeats **until the condition becomes true**. That is the **opposite** question of Python's `while`, which repeats **while** the condition is true. To translate, **flip the condition**: `REPEAT UNTIL(n > 3)` is `while n <= 3:`. Like `while`, the exam checks the condition **before** every pass, so the body can run **zero times**.

What is a while loop?
A while loop repeats its body **as long as a yes-or-no question is `True`**. Python asks the question again before every pass.

Show me step by step
Python sets `count = 1`.
It asks: is `count <= 3`? Yes, so it runs the body: print 1, then `count` becomes 2.
It asks again: 2 <= 3? Yes. Print 2, then `count` becomes 3.
It asks again: 3 <= 3? Yes. Print 3, then `count` becomes 4.
It asks again: 4 <= 3? No. The loop is over, and `print("Done")` runs.

Loop and a Half
What you will learn

In the last lesson every `while` loop had its question at the **top**, and you had to ask for input **twice**: once before the loop and once inside it. The **loop and a half** is a cleaner pattern. `while True:` starts a loop that would run forever, and an `if ...: break` **inside** the loop jumps out when you want to stop. You ask only **once**, and the loop can stop in the **middle** of a pass (that is the "half"). It is perfect for adding up numbers until the user types a **sentinel**, a special value that means stop, and for checking what a user typed.

**On the AP exam:** the exam has **no** `break` and **no** `while True`. It uses `REPEAT UNTIL(condition)`, and it gets the first value **before** the loop and the next value at the **bottom** of the loop. The loop and a half is a **Python skill**, but the exam still asks what a loop **does**, so you will write **both** versions and learn to read either one.

What does while True mean?

`True` is always `True`, so the question never becomes `False`. The loop would run **forever** if nothing stopped it. That is fine, because you add an `if` with a `break` **inside** to stop it when you want.
A `while True:` loop with **no** `break` is an infinite loop.
What does break do?
`break` ends the loop **immediately**. Python skips the rest of the body and continues with the first line **after** the loop (the one that is not indented).

What you will learn

Games, simulations, and shuffled playlists all need **randomness**. Python can pick a random number for you. You **import** the `random` tool at the top, and then `random.randint(1, 6)` rolls a six-sided die: a **whole number from 1 to 6, and both 1 and 6 are possible**. Python's `random.randint(a, b)` works the **same way**: both ends are included. That is different from `range`, which stops **before** its end.

The two kinds of comments

A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code. It is a title for a whole section, like `# Step 3` or `# Ride checker`.

Every other comment goes on the **SAME line** as the code it explains, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`. An explaining comment never goes on its own line above or below.

How do I print words and a number together?
There are two ways. Both give the same result.
1. A comma (the easy way)
Python adds a space between the pieces for you, and it works with any kind of value.
2. Plus and str()
`+` only joins text to text. So a number has to be turned into text first with `str()`. You also have to type the space yourself.
`print("Whole minutes: " + 2)` crashes with a TypeError, because `+` can't join text and a number.
